On July 19, 1892, Congress authorized the construction of “one sea-going coast-line battleship, designed to carry the heaviest armor and most powerful ordnance.” It was designated Battleship Number 4 (BB-4), USS Iowa.

rows.claim: Iowa was designed with a raised forecastle deck to give her more freeboard than the Indiana class, since she had to operate on the high seas rather than just coastal waters. The higher bow kept her main guns workable in heavy weather instead of being swamped.
rows.quote: Her higher freeboard made her a better seagoing battleship than the previous Indiana (BB-1) class, which made the guns easier to work in heavy seas.
rows.passage: Changing public ideas of the true uses of a naval force permitted the building of the Iowa (11,340 tons), which was frankly called a "sea-going battleship." Her higher freeboard made her a better seagoing battleship than the previous Indiana (BB-1) class, which made the guns easier to work in heavy seas.

rows.claim: To buy Iowa's greater freeboard and fuel capacity, designers had to sacrifice gun caliber: the 13-inch main battery used on the Indiana class was swapped for lighter 12-inch guns, trading hitting power to stay within displacement limits.

rows.claim: Maine's two main-gun turrets were sponsoned out on opposite sides of the hull and echeloned, letting both guns fire fore-and-aft for heavy end-on fire in a ramming engagement, a layout borrowed from 1870s Italian designs and HMS Inflexible. The tradeoff was weak broadside fire, a liability in a battle line.
rows.quote: This gun arrangement met the design demand for heavy end-on fire in a ship-to-ship encounter, tactics that involved ramming the enemy vessel.
rows.passage: The practice of en echelon mounting had begun with Italian battleships designed in the 1870s by Benedetto Brin and followed by the British Navy with HMS Inflexible, which was laid down in 1874 but not commissioned until October 1881.[20] This gun arrangement met the design demand for heavy end-on fire in a ship-to-ship encounter, tactics that involved ramming the enemy vessel.[11] The wisdom of this tactic was largely theoretical at the time when it was implemented.

rows.claim: Maine's echeloned turrets sat far apart with no counterbalance, so pointing both guns the same direction made the ship heel over, and cross-deck firing across the superstructure damaged her own deck when tried. The arrangement traded broadside power and stability for theoretical end-on ramming fire, and was abandoned on later designs.

rows.claim: Maine took an unusually protracted nine years to build, partly because her armor plating alone took three years to deliver and a fire in the shipyard drafting room destroyed her working blueprints. The delay was so long that naval tactics shifted underneath her, and her near-sister USS Texas actually entered service before her despite being laid down later.
rows.quote: The delivery of her armored plating took three years, and a fire in the drafting room of the building yard, where Maine's working set of blueprints were stored, caused further delay.

rows.claim: Maine was designed to counter South American ironclads like Riachuelo in a fleet action, but her nine-year build dragged so long that naval tactics and technology moved past her before she ever fought. She is remembered today not for any battle her armament won, but for the 1898 Havana harbor explosion that helped trigger the Spanish-American War.

rows.claim: Maine exploded in Havana harbor on 15 February 1898, killing 266 of her 354 officers and crew - a loss the Navy's official history calls a tragedy that jolted the nation.
rows.quote: Its destruction and the loss of 266 officers and crew was a tragedy that jolted the nation and struck at the heart of the U.S. Navy, which was then a small and close-knit service.

rows.claim: The 1898 Naval Court of Inquiry, convened right after the blast, concluded Maine was destroyed by an external mine/sabotage, a verdict that helped push the US into war with Spain.
rows.quote: it seems to have done its best to arrive at the unbiased verdict that Maine was destroyed by sabotage.

rows.claim: Decades later, Adm. Hyman Rickover's modern study concluded the more likely cause was a spontaneous coal-bunker fire that set off an adjacent magazine, not sabotage.
rows.quote: Maine was destroyed by a spontaneous fire in a coal bunker that set off ammunition stored near-by, a theory strongly supported by the best modern study on the destruction of Maine authored by Adm. Hyman G. Rickover

Congress authorized a new class of battleships as war spread across Europe and Asia. The Navy needed ships with the speed to operate alongside fast aircraft carriers, the range to cross the Pacific, and the firepower and armor expected of a capital ship.
